message.content:
Lions (Panthera leo) belong to the order **Carnivora** (family Felidae), while zebras (Equus quagga) belong to the order **Perissodactyla** (family Equidae).  
The two orders diverged from a common ancestor that is part of the larger clade **Laurasiatheria**.  

So the last common ancestor of a lion and a zebra would have been a small, probably insect‑eating mammal that lived roughly **90 million years ago**, the ancestral stock of Laurasiatheria from which both Carnivora and Perissodactyla later evolved.

The user asks: "What is the common ancestor of lion and zebra?" They want a biological answer. We can provide a general answer: The common ancestor of lions (Panthera leo) and zebras (Equus quagga) would be a common ancestor of the family Felidae and Equidae, which diverged from a common ancestor in the order Carnivora? Wait, zebras are in the order Perissodactyla (odd-toed ungulates). Lions are in Carnivora. So the common ancestor would be at the level of the class Mammalia, maybe at the level of the clade Euarchontoglires? Actually, the common ancestor of all mammals is the ancestor of the clade Mammalia. But we can be more specific: The last common ancestor of lions and zebras would be the last common ancestor of the clades Carnivora and Perissodactyla, which is the ancestor of the clade Laurasiatheria. So the common ancestor would be a mammal that lived around 90 million years ago, the ancestor of Laurasiatheria. So we can answer: The last common ancestor of lions and zebras was a small, probably insectivorous mammal that lived about 90 million years ago, the ancestor of Laurasiatheria. Or we can say: The common ancestor of lions and zebras is the last common ancestor of the clade Laurasiatheria, which includes Carnivora (lions) and Perissodactyla (zebras). So we can answer accordingly.
